newsitem.title: USA: Dow industrials up but off highs at midday.
newsitem.headline: Dow industrials up but off highs at midday.

text.p: Wall Street stocks bounced back Friday in what analysts dubbed a knee-jerk response to Thursday's 160-point plunge, but blue chips slipped off their highs as interest rate fears resurfaced.
The Dow Jones industrial average was up 30.02 points at 6,908.91 at 1 p.m. EST after climbing as high as 6,956.63 earlier.
Advancing issues outnumbered declines 1,330 to 937 on volume of nearly 278 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"This looks like a simple technical rebound after the Dow dropped 160 points yesterday," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co, was sceptical of Friday's bounce.

"It's convincing in neither stocks nor bonds. Taken in aggregate, recent data indicate that the economy is expanding much more rapidly than the Federal Reserve would like. After warning us twice this month, it's likely the Fed will move later this month to tighten credit," he said.
The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25.

Just as Thursday's decline was triggered by surprisingly strong economic data -- strong February retail sales and low weekly jobless claims -- Friday's bounce was sparked by a weaker-than-expected report on February producer prices.
The Producer Price Index fell 0.4 percent, with the core rate down 0.1 percent.
Capacity utilization came in at 83.3 percent, while industrial production rose 0.5 percent, in line with Wall Street expectations.

"The blue chips are still extended by a long way, and they are still vulnerable," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "The stock market hinges on the day-to-day activity of the bond market. If the lond bond yield goes above 7 percent, stocks will get clobbered again."

The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was up an eighth of a point, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, slipped to 6.95 percent from 6.96 percent Thursday, when the bond lost nearly a full point.
"What you are seeing today is simply a response to yesterday's decline," Wachtel said. "People buy on the dips. I think the market will soften by the end of the day."
The Nasdaq Composite Index was up 4.04 points at 1,297.32 despite a decidedly mixed high-technology sector.

Database software power Oracle Corp. was up 4 at 40-1/8 on Nasdaq. Oracle said late Thursday its license sales for the third quarter ending in February were up 29 percent, service sales were up 41 percent and its flagship Oracle8 programme will ship in June.

But Dow component International Business Machines Corp. was up a mere 1/8 at 142-7/8 on the NYSE. Intel Corp. was down 1/4 at 141, Microsoft Corp. was up 1/4 at 99-7/8 and Cisco Systems Inc. was off 1-3/4 at 50-1/4, all on Nasdaq.
"The tech stocks are still lagging very badly and have not been able to regain their status as leaders," said Interstate/Johnson's Harrington.
"This is not a good sign. When the leadership group falters this badly, it's a sign that the overall market might come under similar pressure," Harrington said.

Friday's big loser appeared to be Employee Solutions Inc., the most actively traded Nasdaq issue. The stock was down 9-1/16 at 6-5/16 after the company said fourth-quarter profits would fall below expectations.

The second-biggest loser was Premisys Communications Inc., down 3-1/2 at 7-3/4 after announcing Friday that it expects to lose 10 cents to 14 cents per share in the quarter ending March 31, including a previously announced 9-cent-per-share charge.
